items.question: What does a vaccine present so the immune system can learn to recognize a pathogen?
items.evidence_quote: A vaccine trains your immune system by showing it a safe version or piece of a pathogen so it can learn to recognize and fight the real one later.

items.question: Which cells can remain after the initial vaccine response and help with later recognition?
items.evidence_quote: Some activated B and T cells become long-lived memory cells.

items.question: On a later encounter with the real pathogen, what role do immune memory cells play?
items.evidence_quote: If the real pathogen enters later, these cells help the immune system respond more quickly and effectively.

items.question: What does a vaccine present so the immune system can learn to recognize a pathogen?
items.evidence_quote: A vaccine works by showing your immune system a safe preview of a pathogen, so it can build a response in advance without you ever getting sick.

items.question: Which cells can remain after the initial vaccine response and help with later recognition?
items.evidence_quote: After the response winds down, long-lived memory B and T cells remain, sometimes for decades.

items.question: On a later encounter with the real pathogen, what role do immune memory cells play?
items.evidence_quote: Instead of the slow first-time response, which can take over a week and gives the pathogen a head start, your body responds within hours to days, producing large amounts of antibodies and killer T cells quickly.
